recall_prompt: Say how you would show z satisfies this quadratic without substituting z into it.
insider_note: The short route earns both marks: move the 2 across first, so squaring gives (−3i)² = −9 and the i disappears in one line. Squaring z = 2 − 3i as it stands keeps an i term that never cancels.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Isolate the i and square
steps.margin_note: First mark. Move the 2 to the left so the right side is only −3i, then square: (−3i)² = 9i² = −9. The i is gone.
steps.memory_tip: Move the 2 across first, then square: (−3i)² = −9 and the i is gone in one line.

recall.must_convey: That z − 2 = −3i is squared to give (z − 2)² = −9.
accept: move the two across so z minus two is minus three i, then square to get minus nine
z minus two squared equals minus three i squared equals minus nine
isolate the imaginary part and square both sides
z minus two equals minus three i, square cheste minus nine
square z minus two to remove the i

steps.why: Squaring −3i gives a real number, so z is seen to satisfy a real quadratic in one step. Substituting 2 − 3i into z² − 4z + 13 also works but needs an expansion with cross terms.
common_mistakes: Squaring z = 2 − 3i as it stands, which keeps an i term.

steps.label: Expand and rearrange
steps.margin_note: Second mark. (z − 2)² = z² − 4z + 4. Move the −9 across: 4 + 9 = 13.
steps.memory_tip: The 13 is 4 + 9 — the 4 from squaring the 2, the 9 from squaring the 3.

recall.must_convey: That expanding gives z² − 4z + 4 = −9, so z² − 4z + 13 = 0.
accept: expand to z squared minus four z plus four equals minus nine and move the nine across to get z squared minus four z plus thirteen equals zero
z squared minus four z plus four plus nine is zero, that is plus thirteen
bring minus nine to the left, four plus nine is thirteen

steps.why: The constant 13 is 4 + 9 — the 4 from squaring the 2 and the 9 from squaring the 3. Seeing where 13 comes from is the check that the answer was reached, not copied.
